property_summary: If SetMinSum reverts when called, then intitalized must have been true before the call (i.e., reverting implies the contract was already initialized).
Calling SetMinSum should never revert when it is the first call to SetMinSum on this contract instance (i.e., when no prior SetMinSum call has been made).

After any call to Collect by a holder, MinSum remains unchanged (reference: Collect never modifies MinSum; mutant sets intitalized in SetMinSum causing MinSum to be frozen earlier which can differ after interactions), and the mutant can produce a different MinSum value after Collect for some inputs.

The reference contract never sets intitalized to true when SetMinSum is called (so MinSum can still be later changed by a subsequent SetMinSum before Initialized() is called), whereas the mutant makes the first SetMinSum call freeze MinSum by setting intitalized=true; thus: for any fuzzed actor and value, calling SetMinSum once then calling SetLogFile and Initialized() should leave MinSum equal to the last-set value only in the reference for all admissible inputs, while the mutant can cause MinSum to be frozen earlier and differ (we test that calling SetMinSum twice with two fuzzed values leaves MinSum equal to the second value in the reference but may not in the mutant).
After initialization is prevented, setting MinSum with SetMinSum(_val) results in MinSum equal to the provided _val (not forcibly zero).
If contract C is not initialized, calling SetMinSum(v) sets MinSum to v (i.e., MinSum equals the argument passed).
After calling SetMinSum(x) once before Initialized(), the public MinSum equals the provided x (i.e. MinSum == x).
After calling SetMinSum with any nonzero sender (normal externally-owned account), MinSum becomes that value (i.e., SetMinSum succeeds for non-zero callers).
SetMinSum can only succeed when called by the zero address in the mutant, so for any non-zero caller SetMinSum must NOT revert in the original contract (i.e., calls by non-zero addresses succeed).
Calling SetMinSum once before Initialized succeeds (does not revert) and makes MinSum equal to the input value.
Calling SetMinSum should never revert when the contract has not been initialized; i.e., if Initialized() has not yet been called, SetMinSum(...) must succeed.
Before initialization, SetMinSum must be callable (not revert) allowing MinSum to be set; after calling Initialized(), SetMinSum reverts.
SetMinSum is callable (does not revert) exactly when the contract has not yet been initialized.

For any input _val and before Initialized() is called, calling SetMinSum(_val) causes the contract's MinSum to equal the provided _val (the reference preserves the argument); the mutant that stores 0 breaks this rule for any _val != 0.

For any input value _val, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the correct contract stores MinSum equal to the provided value; the mutant stores the bitwise complement (~_val) so this equality is violated for inputs where _val != ~_val (i.e. most values).

After calling SetLogFile(x) before Initialized, the contract's LogFile getter equals the provided address x for every input; the mutant that always sets LogFile to address(0) violates this for any x != address(0).

For any address addr passed to SetLogFile before Initialized, the contract's public LogFile getter returns that same address (i.e., LogFile == addr); the mutant that always sets LogFile to address(0) violates this whenever addr != address(0).

For any address a passed to SetLogFile before initialization, calling SetLogFile(a) and then Initialized() leaves LogFile as a non-zero address in the reference (specifically equal to the provided address when it is non-zero), whereas the mutant that casts to address(0) will make LogFile zero for some non-zero a (so the invariant that LogFile != address(0) after setting with a non-zero a is broken).

For every non-zero address A passed to SetLogFile before Initialized(), the contract's LogFile public getter returns a non-zero address (specifically the same address A) after the call; the mutant that forces LogFile to address(0) breaks this by returning zero for some non-zero A.

For every address arg passed to SetLogFile before the contract is Initialized, calling SetLogFile succeeds (does not revert) and leaves c.LogFile() referring to a contract whose Address is non-zero iff the provided address hosts a deployed contract; the mutant always writes address(0) and thus for some inputs (a deployed contract address) the getter differs.

For any input address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract always sets the public LogFile getter to the same _log value (even if zero); the mutant leaves LogFile unchanged when _log is address(0), so for some inputs (e.g. when _log == address(0)) the stored LogFile differs from the passed value.

For any address input _log, after calling SetLogFile(_log) the contract's public LogFile getter equals the passed address (i.e., SetLogFile always assigns LogFile to _log); the mutant skips assignment when _log == address(0) so this rule is violated for the zero address.

For every input address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) results in the contract's public LogFile getter returning _log (the reference always assigns the value, the mutant refuses to assign when _log == address(0) causing a mismatch).

For every caller and address input _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the reference contract makes the public LogFile getter reflect the provided address (i.e. the stored LogFile equals _log); the mutant sometimes leaves LogFile unchanged when _log == address(0), breaking this equality for that input.

For every address _log and caller, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the reference always updates the public LogFile getter to _log; the mutant fails to update when _log == address(0), leaving LogFile unchanged (so the getter can differ), so the property is that after SetLogFile(_log) the stored LogFile equals _log.

For any caller and log address, calling SetLogFile on the correct contract never changes LogFile when Initialized() has already been called (call reverts before assignment), whereas the mutant assigns LogFile before reverting and thus can change the stored LogFile for some inputs.

After C.Initialized() has been called, any call to SetLogFile(_) must revert without changing the stored LogFile; the mutant assigns LogFile before reverting, so for some addresses SetLogFile returns ok=true (or leaves LogFile changed) whereas the reference always reverts and leaves LogFile untouched.

After Initialized() is called, any SetLogFile(address) call must either revert and leave LogFile unchanged for the reference contract; the mutant may assign LogFile before reverting for some callee addresses, so there exist inputs where LogFile changes despite the call ultimately reverting.

For any address provided to SetLogFile after Initialized() has been called, the reference C always reverts and thus preserves the previous LogFile value (call returns false in a try/catch), whereas the mutant may perform the assignment before reverting causing the stored LogFile to change or the call to appear to succeed for some addresses; we assert that SetLogFile call always reverts (ok==false) after Initialized().

After calling Initialized(), any SetLogFile(address) call on the correct contract either reverts and leaves LogFile unchanged; the mutant can assign LogFile before reverting when the provided address is a contract whose constructor or conversion to Log does not revert, so there exist inputs (a contract address) where the stored LogFile differs — we assert that SetLogFile ALWAYS reverts (ok == false) after Initialized().

For any caller address and provided _log address, the correct contract sets LogFile to the supplied _log (i.e., c.LogFile() == _log) after SetLogFile is called before initialization; the mutant sets it to msg.sender instead, violating this when caller != _log.

For any caller and provided address _log, the correct contract sets LogFile to the provided _log after SetLogFile is called (i.e., c.LogFile() == _log); the mutant instead sets it to msg.sender, so whenever caller != _log the mutant violates this rule.

For any caller and any supplied address _log, after calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract, LogFile() equals the supplied _log; the mutant instead sets LogFile() to the caller (msg.sender), so whenever caller != _log the mutant violates this rule.

For any caller A and provided address L, after calling SetLogFile(L) on the correct contract, the stored LogFile equals L (i.e., c.LogFile() == L); the mutant instead assigns LogFile = msg.sender, so when caller A != L the mutant violates this rule.

For any caller and any supplied address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract stores _log as LogFile (c.LogFile() == _log); the mutant instead stores msg.sender, so whenever caller != _log the mutant violates this rule.

For any non-initialized contract, calling SetLogFile(address) sets the public LogFile getter to that address; the mutant that deletes the assignment leaves LogFile unchanged for some input address, violating this rule.

For any address A passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the correct contract sets its public LogFile getter to A; the mutant that omits the assignment will leave LogFile unchanged for some A, so the equality address(c.LogFile()) == A can fail.

For any address addr passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference contract sets the public LogFile to addr (address(c.LogFile()) == addr); the mutant that omits the assignment can leave LogFile unchanged for some addr, violating this property.

For any non-initialized call to SetLogFile(addr) the reference contract sets its public LogFile to addr (so address(c.LogFile()) == addr always holds); the mutant that deletes the assignment breaks this because after the call the getter may remain the old value (not equal to addr) for some addr.

For any non-initialized contract C and any address a, calling SetLogFile(a) returns (does not revert) and makes the public LogFile getter report that address (address(c.LogFile()) == a); the mutant that removes the assignment breaks this because after the call the getter can remain a different address.

After calling Put via fallback or Put with zero value, the holder's balance for msg.sender must remain equal to the contract's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance (i.e., zero-value calls do not change balance) — in P zero-value Put is allowed and thus leaves balance unchanged but logs may be added; in M zero-value Put reverts preventing the call.

property_summary: Calling Put with zero msg.value does not revert (i.e., zero-value Put calls succeed) on the original contract.

After any successful Put(...) by an account, the holder's unlockTime is set to the maximum of its previous unlockTime and block.timestamp + _lockTime (i.e., unlockTime never decreases); the mutant flips the comparison and can decrease unlockTime for some inputs.

After any Put by an account, the account's unlockTime is never decreased: reference C ensures acc.unlockTime >= previous value (max of prev and block.timestamp+_lockTime); the mutant uses '<' and can decrease unlockTime for some inputs.

For any caller and any Put(_lockTime) call, the reference contract never decreases that caller's unlockTime (new unlockTime >= previous unlockTime); the mutant with '<' can decrease unlockTime for some inputs, so there exists a fuzzed _lockTime and timing that makes mutant set a smaller unlockTime.

For any caller and any Put(_lockTime) call, the reference contract never decreases that caller's stored unlockTime (it sets unlockTime to max(prev, block.timestamp+_lockTime)), whereas the mutant can decrease unlockTime when it uses '<' and assigns a smaller value.
